4.38180,50.84380.name: Emergency measures — withdrawing an approved organism
4.38180,50.84380.state: Brussels — European Commission, health and food safety
4.38180,50.84380.desc: A member state can suspend or prohibit an already-authorised organism on its territory where new information indicates a risk, and must notify the Commission with its reasons. It has been used, and the safeguard clause invoked this way is what eventually produced the EU opt-out. Two things make it hard: it needs new information rather than a change of mind, and the burden of assembling that information falls on the state invoking it — which is where independent published work matters more than correspondence.

6.14000,46.22250.name: EC — Biotech — caution as a trade barrier
6.14000,46.22250.desc: The United States, Canada and Argentina brought a WTO complaint against the EU’s de facto moratorium on approvals, and the panel found in 2006 that the delays breached the agreement on sanitary measures. It did not rule on whether engineered crops are safe. What it established is that a slow approval process is itself actionable in trade law, which is why a country weighing a restriction is also weighing a dispute.

-3.26800,55.94270.name: Royal Zoological Society of Scotland — WildGenes
-3.26800,55.94270.desc: A conservation genetics laboratory inside a zoo, and the point where two biobanking networks meet: it is simultaneously a CryoArks storage hub and the United Kingdom hub of the European zoo association's biobank, holding up to forty thousand frozen samples per ultra-cold freezer and processing donations and outgoing loan requests. It is worth recording because the practical questions in this facet are logistical rather than philosophical: who accepts a sample, on what terms, who may request it later, and who does the freezing. The answers here are a charity, a shared standard and two freezers in Edinburgh.

1.15600,43.80600.name: Ecocert
1.15600,43.80600.desc: Certification is the mechanism by which a crop is declared free of engineered material, and this map holds 144 rows naming who certifies without naming the largest of them. Ecocert began as a control body spun out of a French organic advisers' association in 1991, and now operates through some 27 to 30 subsidiaries in more than 130 countries; it reports inspecting around 70% of the French organic sector and about 30% worldwide. It grew partly by acquisition — the Institute for Marketecology in 2013, IMOgroup in 2014, and a US certifier in 2019 — and is controlled by the family holding company of its co-founder. Two things follow. A grower in most countries deals with a local subsidiary of a multinational rather than a body founded where they farm. And the EU stopped accepting organic certification on raw Indian cotton from several major certifiers including this one, after fraudulent certificates — the check on the supply chain failing in the same way the supply chain does.
